verses.text: Then Job answered,
“Oh that my anguish were weighed, and all my calamity laid in the balances!
For now it would be heavier than the sand of the seas, therefore have my words been rash.
For the arrows of the Almighty are within me. My spirit drinks up their poison. The terrors of God set themselves in array against me.
Does the wild donkey bray when he has grass? Or does the ox low over his fodder?
Can that which has no flavor be eaten without salt? Or is there any taste in the white of an egg?
My soul refuses to touch them. They are as loathsome food to me.
“Oh that I might have my request, that God would grant the thing that I long for,
even that it would please God to crush me; that he would let loose his hand, and cut me off!
Be it still my consolation, yes, let me exult in pain that doesn’t spare, that I have not denied the words of the Holy One.
What is my strength, that I should wait? What is my end, that I should be patient?
Is my strength the strength of stones? Or is my flesh of brass?
Isn’t it that I have no help in me, That wisdom is driven quite from me?
“To him who is ready to faint, kindness should be shown from his friend; even to him who forsakes the fear of the Almighty.
My brothers have dealt deceitfully as a brook, as the channel of brooks that pass away;
Which are black by reason of the ice, in which the snow hides itself.
In the dry season, they vanish. When it is hot, they are consumed out of their place.
The caravans that travel beside them turn aside. They go up into the waste, and perish.
The caravans of Tema looked. The companies of Sheba waited for them.
They were distressed because they were confident. They came there, and were confounded.
For now you are nothing. You see a terror, and are afraid.
Did I say, ‘Give to me?’ or, ‘Offer a present for me from your substance?’
or, ‘Deliver me from the adversary’s hand?’ or, ‘Redeem me from the hand of the oppressors?’
“Teach me, and I will hold my peace. Cause me to understand wherein I have erred.
How forcible are words of uprightness! But your reproof, what does it reprove?
Do you intend to reprove words, since the speeches of one who is desperate are as wind?
Yes, you would even cast lots for the fatherless, and make merchandise of your friend.
Now therefore be pleased to look at me, for surely I shall not lie to your face.
Please return. Let there be no injustice. Yes, return again. My cause is righteous.
Is there injustice on my tongue? Can’t my taste discern mischievous things?

footnotes.content: Job opens his response—not with argument but with the weight of suffering itself. When a person has borne enough, the words come as a kind of desperate plea to be truly heard. I've learned that listening to the grieving matters more than having answers ready.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Job wishes his pain could be measured and weighed—as if there were scales that could prove it real. In his longing to make the invisible visible, I see how suffering can feel unseen, unwitnessed. Even now, the Lord measures our tears.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He compares his calamity to the sand of the seas—a measure that recalls Abraham's blessing and echoes of God's abundance, now inverted to weight and heaviness. When he says his words have been rash, he owns the consequence of agony: desperation makes us speak before we think. In that honesty lies a strange humility.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The arrows of the Almighty are within me"—Job feels God's judgment as embedded, inescapable. He does not doubt God's power; he feels crushed by it. This is the cry of one who knows the Lord is real and fears He has turned His face away.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A wild donkey bray when there is no grass—or an ox cry over empty fodder? Job appeals to nature itself: the animal only calls out when want is real. He wants his friends to understand his complaint springs not from ingratitude or sin but from genuine need. Even creation teaches us: a cry means something is wrong.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Flavorless food, the pale white of an egg—Job speaks of what is tasteless, empty, without savor. His suffering has made him unable to accept easy comfort. Sometimes a soul grows too tender for shallow words; only truth, only presence, can reach it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His very soul refuses the counsel his friends offer—it has become loathsome to him. He will not be soothed with bromides. I think of how the grieving sometimes push away what is meant as kindness; their refusal is not rejection but a measure of how deep the wound cuts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Job dares to voice what he most longs for—his request before God. There is courage in naming desire, even a dark one. To ask God for anything is still to address God; the prayer is not false even when it asks for what we think we should not want.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He wishes God would crush him and let loose His hand—end it. The cry reveals a soul exhausted beyond measure, seeing death as mercy. Yet Job remains alive, speaking, wrestling. The Lord, in His silence, keeps Job in the land of the living even when Job begs for release.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even in anguish, Job sees consolation: that he has not denied the words of the Holy One. Amid everything, he clings to the truth he knows—that God speaks, that God's word endures. This is the faith of a breaking heart: not joy, but a refusal to abandon what is real.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: What is my strength, that I should wait? Job questions his own endurance. When a person has run through their reserves, hope itself becomes a stranger. Yet the asking is itself a sign—he has not stopped reaching toward God, even in doubt.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He asks if his strength is stone or brass—inhuman, unyielding. The answer is no: he is flesh, breakable, mortal. In naming what he is not, Job speaks the truth of our condition: we are made of something tender, and this tenderness is not weakness but our nature.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wisdom has been driven quite from him. Job feels stripped of discernment and resource alike. In our empty moments, when counsel fails and strength is gone, we learn a strange lesson: we learn to wait. The Lord comes not with wisdom but with Himself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "To him who is ready to faint, kindness should be shown from his friend"—Job cites what ought to be true, what justice and love require. He names the standard his friends have not met. Yet he speaks it without bitterness toward them, as if reminding them what they have forgotten to be.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His brothers have dealt deceitfully as a brook—here is a desert picture: a wadi that flows in rains but dries when you need it most. Job has watched those he counted on disappear when he needed them. In arid lands, such broken streams are a bitter teaching about seasons and faithlessness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Black with ice, the snow hidden in the channel—Job's imagery speaks of winter's darkness, of the season when the brook freezes and conceals. Even when his friends could have watered his thirst, they were locked in their own coldness. There is poetry in his pain.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the dry season they vanish—when heat comes and you need water most, the brook is consumed out of its place. The image captures how reliefs fail us when the pressure is greatest. Job knows this rhythm of nature and speaks it as a picture of broken friendship.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Caravans that travel beside them turn aside—they see no water and abandon the route. Job draws from the caravan trade routes of the Arabian desert, where travelers depended on reliable streams. His friends, like those caravans, have turned away from him when they found no comfort. The wilderness knows such abandonment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Caravans of Tema, companies of Sheba—real trade routes and peoples. Job names them not as generality but as those who knew these brooklands and looked for water. The specificity makes the betrayal real: this is not abstract loneliness but the concrete failure of those in his world.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They were confident and came there and were confounded—they had expected sustenance and found nothing. Job identifies with both the expectation and the shame of disappointment. To trust and be betrayed is a wound deeper than to fear and be vindicated.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now you are nothing—you see my terror and are afraid. Job turns to his friends directly: they have become helpless in the face of his suffering. Perhaps they too are confounded by what they cannot fix. He does not excuse them, but he speaks a truth: sometimes those who wish to help are themselves undone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Did I ask you for gift or ransom? Job has not demanded payment or reward from his friends. He only sought comfort, not commerce. In his refusal to have asked for much, he shows how low his expectations had grown—he wanted only to be heard, not resourced.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Deliver me from the adversary's hand, redeem me from oppressors—Job names what might have been a reasonable request. Yet even these he did not ask. His silence in his need speaks louder than all his reasonable requests could have. Sometimes the grieving ask for nothing because asking itself feels like a burden.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Teach me, and I will hold my peace—Job pivots. If his friends have wisdom, let them speak it. He offers them a bargain: instruction in exchange for silence. There is a strange gentleness here, as if he is trying to meet them partway, to find some ground where they might truly help.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: How forcible are words of uprightness!—he acknowledges the power of truth spoken plainly. But then: your reproof, what does it reprove? Job questions whether what his friends offer is truth at all or merely the appearance of it. Mere words without compassion are hollow instruments.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The speeches of one who is desperate are as wind—Job turns their words back on them. When someone is drowning, is it right to critique the rhythm of their thrashing? His desperation is not the fault of reason but of circumstance. He asks them to account for context, not just correct the words.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You would even cast lots for the fatherless, make merchandise of your friend—Job accuses them of heartlessness. To treat the vulnerable as commodity, to barter friendship as goods: this is the depth of their faithlessness. He sees in their reproof not justice but cruelty dressed as counsel.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Look at me, for surely I shall not lie to your face—Job appeals to them to see him truly, to recognize his sincerity. He will not deceive them. In offering his honest presence, he makes a final plea: let me be known as I am.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Return, let there be no injustice—Job asks them to turn back, to reconsider. He stands by his cause as righteous, not guilty as they have judged. Yet he speaks with restraint, asking for return rather than demanding vindication. There is a dignity in his sorrow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Is there injustice on my tongue? Readers today hear an echo of every honest person who has been disbelieved, who has spoken truth and been called liar by those who should have known them. In Job's question, we recognize ourselves—the ache of being wrongly accused by those we thought understood us. It is a wound that has not aged since Job's day.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
